What is the "steering" versus "learning" subsystem in Byrnes’ work?

Where is each sensory modality "wired in?" This dictates cortical organization (the spatial distribution of representations (e.g abstraction gradients and cross-modal hubs)).

Structure-function coupling in the human brainstem

Evolution didn’t replace the old predictive systems (cerebellum for forward models, BG for value-based selection), it added a third prediction engine that operates at a different timescale and level of abstraction. The cerebellum predicts immediate sensory consequences of actions (microsecond-to-second range), the cortex builds hierarchical models of the world structure and long-term contingencies, and the BG sits in between, using both to steer behavior toward rewarding states. By the time you get to primates around 50-60 million years ago, cortex has exploded to dominate brain volume–humans are  75% cortex by mass. That’s the system doing the heavy lifting on abstract world modeling in modern mammals.

Evolution built the vertebrate brain by accretion rather than replacement. The hypothalamus and brainstem are the ancient core that keeps an animal alive, coupling interoceptive signals to autonomic, endocrine, and instinctive behavioral responses; their circuitry integrates peripheral state and sets homeostatic goals such as thermoregulation, energy balance, and arousal 2, 3. In mammals, these nuclei remain small in volume but disproportionately powerful levers on behavior, coordinating visceral reflexes with motivated action. They are the control room for set-points, not a relic, and they still dictate the "why now?" of behavior. A recent anatomical illustration locates the major subdivisions (Figure) 21. A recent preprint supplies a complementary view of subcortical loops (Figure) 22.

Layered on top is the telencephalon’s dorsal pallium, which in mammals expanded into the six-layered neocortex-an evolutionary novelty that scaled dramatically in primates. Strip away the folds and the human cortex is only a few millimeters thick (roughly 2-4 mm, mean  2.5 mm) 4, yet-depending on method and sample-its sheet spans on the order of 1,600-2,500 cm² when flattened; the exact figure varies with how much buried sulcal surface you count. What matters for computation is the sheet’s repeating microcircuit theme 5: thalamic "driver" inputs preferentially target layer IV; layers II/III broadcast cortico-cortically; layers V/VI drive subcortical targets. The motif is conserved but not rigid: primary motor cortex is famously agranular or near-agranular (weak layer 4) 6, yet recent physiology shows a small, functionally bona fide L4-like relay there. Across areas, the "canonical" circuit is less a blueprint than a grammar that supports specialization through changes in input-output statistics and interneuron composition.

Cortex does not operate in isolation; it is wired around thalamus. A core organizational principle is the cortico-thalamo-cortical loop, which comes in two flavors. First-order relays (e.g., LGN) carry subcortical drivers to cortex; higher-order relays are driven by cortex itself (often from layer 5 "driver" neurons) and route messages between cortical areas via the thalamus ("trans-thalamic" communication). The pulvinar-enlarged in primates alongside visual and association cortex-illustrates the point: it synchronizes and gates traffic among connected cortical maps according to attentional demands, acting as a flexible switchboard rather than a passive relay 7, 8. These laminar and thalamic asymmetries implement a directional grammar: supragranular-heavy feedforward pathways convey sensory evidence up hierarchies, while infragranular-heavy feedback conveys predictions, context, and goals back down.

The large-scale picture of cortex is often caricatured as "uniform," but "uniformly reconfigurable" is more accurate. The sheet uses the same laminar parts list to build distinct mesoscale specializations 5-granular primary sensory areas dominated by thalamic drive; intermediate association zones that remix multimodal features; and agranular premotor/prefrontal zones that emit deep-layer commands and predictions. This graded architecture explains why feedforward/feedback dynamics and oscillatory regimes change smoothly across space and task, without appealing to different learning rules per area 9.

By contrast, subcortical systems are anatomical one-offs-compact, deeply conserved "coprocessors" with idiosyncratic algorithms that the cortex recruits via re-entrant loops 10. The basal ganglia concentrate massive cortical and thalamic convergence into a small set of tonic output channels that can disinhibit brainstem controllers and motor thalamus; their parallel, partially segregated cortico-BG-thalamo-cortical loops implement selection and dopaminergically gated credit assignment 11, 12. The canonical architecture-motor, associative, limbic loops running in parallel with a ventral-to-dorsal "ascending spiral" via midbrain dopamine-provides a literal pathway for value to bias policy and for habits to crystallize.

The cerebellum is the timing/forecasting counterpart to the basal ganglia’s selection/valuation machinery. It is neuron-dense ( 69-70 billion neurons,  80% of all brain neurons, mostly granule cells 13) yet small in mass, and it connects to cortex through closed-loop cerebro-cerebellar circuits via the pons and thalamus 14, 15. These loops are topographically matched: the same cortical fields that send a mossy-fiber copy of their commands receive refined predictions back, enabling rapid calibration of sensorimotor sequences and, in association territories, the timing of cognitive operations such as working memory and planning.

Two allocortical (the phylogenetically oldest part of the cerebral cortex, characterized by fewer than six cell layers) systems round out the telencephalic toolbox. The hippocampal formation (archicortex) is optimized for rapid relational binding and episodic indexing, enabling one-shot learning of who-did-what-where-when and the recombination of those relations during simulation and planning 16. The amygdala (especially BLA) attaches valence/arousal to stimuli and events and recruits neuromodulatory systems (basal forebrain ACh, locus coeruleus NE) to increase gain and plasticity for behaviorally important inputs 17. These systems are not "limbic add-ons"; they are bidirectionally coupled with multimodal cortex and subcortical drivers and reshape processing on the fly. Single-nucleus sequencing identifies a distinct amygdalostriatal transition-zone cell population (Figure) 20. Amygdalostriatal transition-zone neurons sustain activity during threat-predictive cues (Figure).

If you step back, the brain’s broad subdivisions form a three-tier information-flow hierarchy that evolution has tuned rather than redesigned. The homeostatic and orienting tier (hypothalamus-brainstem-superior colliculus) provides the organism’s internal objectives and fast reflexive reorienting. The valuation/selection/timing tier (basal ganglia, cerebellum, amygdala) assigns priorities, selects policies, and calibrates temporal structure. The representational/predictive tier (cortex with its thalamic relays, plus hippocampal indexing) builds and queries compositional world models under those priorities. What makes primate-and especially human-brains distinctive is not a brand-new module, but the scale and coupling 18: a massively expanded cortical mantle ( 75-84% of brain mass, depending on inclusion of white matter) riding on conserved subcortical loops, with an enlarged pulvinar and association thalamus to orchestrate long-range cortical communication 19. That combination buys depth, bandwidth, and flexible arbitration without discarding the reliable, fast machinery underneath.
